muesli_review.source: Local checkout inspected read-only, alongside public GitHub README.
findings: Go/pgx backend with externally configured PostgreSQL for hosting.
Embedded mode starts and supervises a real local PostgreSQL instance.
Packaged Electron resources supply pinned PostgreSQL binaries.
Local code has credential persistence, directory ownership locking, startup recovery and shutdown handling.
The inspected desktop assembly script explicitly wires darwin-arm64 and linux-x64; Windows packaging was not verified.
The inspected embedded configuration targets PostgreSQL 17; this spike used PostgreSQL 18.6. Major-version alignment and upgrade handling require an explicit decision.

sample.method: Seeded byte-region cluster sample, with target stream weights proportional to live entry counts; duplicate occurrence IDs are excluded. This is a search-layout experiment, not an unbiased statistical sample or full-edition capacity test.

versions.postgres: PostgreSQL 18.6 on aarch64-unknown-linux-musl, compiled by gcc (Alpine 15.2.0) 15.2.0, 64-bit

limitations: Two-million-row byte-region cluster sample from the 2005 edition, not the complete dataset.
Warm local Docker runs, no public-network latency or cold-cache capacity claims.
Flat fourteen-column prototype omits full production provenance payload and fuzzy address search.
PostgreSQL has a separate database container and TCP hop; SQLite and DuckDB are embedded in the client container. Absolute engine rankings are not a controlled equal-total-resource comparison.
Each engine/client container is capped at two CPUs and 1 GiB; DuckDB memory limit 512 MiB and two threads.
Closed-loop concurrent readers; bounded pool/arrival-rate behaviour is measured separately by the Go HTTP spike.
Parquet uses four full sorted copies and query routing to the most favourable copy; file sizes include all four.

notes: Go HTTP client and backend run in separate two-CPU/1-GiB containers on the same machine.
PostgreSQL and Go API share one backend container; SQLite and Go API share the other.
Warm two-million-row sample; this is not an internet or full-dataset capacity result.
Every response body is checked against a previously field-validated reference hash.
HTTP transfer, body-hash validation and database connection-pool waits are included; the load generator does not parse response JSON.

http_correctness.field_comparisons: Every returned field compared with the SQLite SQL reference

limitations: Candidate-name generation only; does not include fetching and ranking matching occurrences.
Warm sample dictionary, not the complete multi-edition dictionary.
Logical custom-format dump restored into a fresh database on the same PostgreSQL version and architecture.
This does not test native macOS/Windows packaging, first-launch time, or cross-version upgrades.
Dump/restore runs used the two-CPU/1-GiB PostgreSQL container.
data_pack.hash_check_method: Count and sum of PostgreSQL hashtextextended(row(e.*)::text,0) over all rows/columns, same engine/version; non-cryptographic aggregate check.

limitations: This is a short engineering spike, not a production capacity certification.
Two million unique occurrences from the 2005 edition: about 3.9% of that edition and 1.1% of all currently supported occurrences.
The sample uses seeded byte-region clusters and excludes duplicate occurrence IDs. It is not an unbiased population sample.
The prototype has fourteen flattened columns. It omits the full production provenance/warning payload and several source fields; production storage must be measured again.

HTTP tests repeatedly exercised 210 common/rare exact and prefix query cases, limited to 50 rows, with warm caches. Broad unseen-key, cold-cache, deep-pagination and full multi-edition behaviour were not measured.
Each closed-loop level lasted five seconds; scheduled-arrival tests sent 500 requests at 100 requests/second. These timings are too short to establish long-running capacity or operational stability.
HTTP service and load generator used separate containers. Each backend was limited to two CPU quotas and 1 GiB memory; this is a Docker Desktop ARM64 test, not a target-VPS hardware test.
Both Go services used eight database connections and a 64-request admission cap. Tests reached 32 simultaneous callers; overload beyond that cap was not exercised.
The load generator validates response bytes against field-checked reference hashes. Its HTTP measurements include transport, body validation and pool waits, while excluding client JSON parsing.
DuckDB/Parquet was tested through its Python SQL interface, rather than the Go HTTP endpoint. Its timings cannot be directly ranked against Go HTTP timings.
The raw Python multithreaded SQLite measurements differed substantially from the common-Go HTTP measurements. Their cause was not isolated; use the Go HTTP test for application comparisons.
Parquet had four full Zstandard-compressed sorted copies, with routing to the favourable copy for each query. The storage total includes all four.
The surname trigram experiment measures candidate-name generation only. Fetching/ranking matching occurrences and full fuzzy-address queries were not benchmarked.
SQLite and Parquet preparation ran on the uncapped native host. PostgreSQL preparation and data-pack dump/restore ran in the capped database container, with a native-host preparation client.
Data-pack restore was tested on the same PostgreSQL version/architecture. Native desktop startup, Windows distribution, relocation and major-version upgrade paths remain untested.
Rust was not benchmarked; this spike provides no evidence that a Rust rewrite would improve the service.

recommendation.initial_implementation: Go + PostgreSQL for both hosted and embedded desktop modes, following the existing Muesli architecture. A shared Electron/React UI can use the same HTTP contract.
recommendation.reason: Both SQL engines performed well in the tested read workload. PostgreSQL allows a shared schema/query/migration path and reuses an existing desktop operational pattern; performance does not compel separate desktop storage.
recommendation.parquet: Useful for columnar analysis/export if required. The measured PostgreSQL logical pack also provides a compact bootstrap path, so Parquet is optional for the initial serving implementation.
recommendation.python: Keep the validated Python reader as the source importer/reference. Porting four binary decoders is not a prerequisite for a Go serving backend.
recommendation.schema: Build an edition-aware occurrence model, preserve raw display/provenance/warnings, and measure a lean indexed search projection with separate detail/address/name dictionaries. Trigram candidate generation can use unique names instead of indexing every occurrence.
recommendation.next_gate: Complete one full-edition production schema/index build and a sustained cold/warm load test on the intended VPS; test native desktop first-launch import, offline restart, relocation and crash cleanup.
